# AGENTS.md for the Infrastructure layer

These rules apply to code in `src/Infrastructure`, in addition to the root `AGENTS.md`. They cover data access with EF Core.

## What lives here

- `Persistence/`: the `DbContext`, one `IEntityTypeConfiguration` class per entity, and the migrations.
- One folder per feature (for example `Todos/`) with the implementations of the interfaces that the application layer defines.
- `InfrastructureServiceRegistration.cs`: the only public type. Everything else is `internal`.

The sample uses SQLite so that it runs without a database server. The rules below apply to any relational provider unless they say otherwise.

## Boundaries

- Keep the `DbContext`, the configurations, and the repositories `internal`. Why: other layers then cannot query the database directly, even by accident. The compiler enforces this, and an architecture test checks that `Api` does not use EF Core.
- Do not return `IQueryable<T>` or `DbSet<T>` from a repository. Return entities, DTOs, or lists. Why: a leaked `IQueryable` lets callers build queries outside this layer, where nobody reviews the SQL.
- Map entities in `IEntityTypeConfiguration` classes, not with attributes on the entity. Why: the domain layer must not depend on EF Core.
- Do not add public setters or a public parameterless constructor to an entity to make EF Core happy. EF Core can use private constructors and read-only properties when the configuration names them. See `TodoItemConfiguration.cs`.

## Queries

- Use `AsNoTracking()` on every query whose result is only read. Why: change tracking costs memory and time, and it is only needed when the entity will be saved again. Source: [Tracking vs. no-tracking queries](https://learn.microsoft.com/ef/core/querying/tracking).
- Load an entity with a tracked query when the use case changes it and saves it.
- Filter, sort, and page in the database. Do not call `ToListAsync()` and then filter in memory. Why: that loads the whole table into the application.
- Select only what the caller needs. For read models, project to a DTO with `Select` instead of loading whole entities. Source: [Efficient querying](https://learn.microsoft.com/ef/core/performance/efficient-querying).
- Never run a query inside a loop over the results of another query (the N+1 problem). Load related data in the same query with `Include` or a projection.
- When a query includes more than one collection, decide between a single query and `AsSplitQuery()` on purpose, and say why in a comment.
- Give every list query a deterministic `OrderBy` and a limit. Why: without a limit, the query grows with the table.

## Async

- Use the async methods (`ToListAsync`, `SingleOrDefaultAsync`, `SaveChangesAsync`) and pass the `CancellationToken` to each of them.
- Never call `.Result` or `.Wait()` on a database call.
- Do not run two operations on the same `DbContext` at the same time, for example with `Task.WhenAll`. Why: a `DbContext` is not thread-safe.

## Raw SQL

- Prefer LINQ. Use raw SQL only when LINQ cannot express the query, and say why in a comment.
- Never build SQL by concatenating or interpolating user input into `FromSqlRaw` or `ExecuteSqlRaw`. Use `FromSql` or `ExecuteSql` with an interpolated string, which turns the values into parameters. Source: [SQL queries](https://learn.microsoft.com/ef/core/querying/sql-queries).

## Migrations

- Every change to an entity or its configuration needs a migration in the same pull request. The test `MigrationsMatchTheModel` fails when one is missing.
- Add a migration with the local tool, from the repository root:

  ```bash
  dotnet tool restore
  dotnet ef migrations add <Name> --project src/Infrastructure --startup-project src/Infrastructure --framework net10.0 --output-dir Persistence/Migrations
  dotnet format
  ```

  `dotnet format` is needed because the generated code does not follow the style rules of this repository, and warnings are errors.
- Read the generated migration before committing it. Why: a rename is often generated as a drop and an add, which deletes data.
- Never edit or delete a migration that has been merged into `main`. Add a new migration instead. Why: databases that already applied the old one would no longer match the code.
- Do not write the model snapshot by hand. The tool owns it.
- The API applies migrations at startup in the Development environment only. In production, apply them as a separate deployment step. Source: [Applying migrations](https://learn.microsoft.com/ef/core/managing-schemas/migrations/applying).
- Both target frameworks share one set of migrations. Generate them with `--framework net10.0`, the lower EF Core version, so they compile and run on both. The integration tests run the migrations on both frameworks.

## Connection strings

- Read the connection string from configuration. `Api` passes it to `AddInfrastructure`.
- The connection string in `appsettings.json` is a local SQLite file name and contains no secret. Never commit a connection string with a password. Use user secrets or environment variables for real values.

## SQLite specifics

- SQLite cannot compare or sort `DateTimeOffset`, `decimal`, or `TimeSpan` values in SQL. A query that tries throws at run time. Source: [SQLite provider limitations](https://learn.microsoft.com/ef/core/providers/sqlite/limitations). If you need such a query, say so instead of sorting in memory.
- SQLite does not enforce `HasMaxLength`. Length rules are enforced by the domain entity.

## Tests

- Test data access against a real database, not the EF Core in-memory provider. Why: the in-memory provider does not run SQL, so it hides translation errors and constraint violations. The integration tests create a temporary SQLite file and apply the migrations to it.
- Save with one `DbContext` and read with another, so the test proves the data reached the database.

## Opinions

These are choices of this playbook, not facts about EF Core. Adapt them to your team.

- A repository per feature in front of the `DbContext`. Some teams use the `DbContext` directly in the application layer. That is a valid trade, but it lets EF Core into `Application`, which this sample forbids.
- Repositories call `SaveChangesAsync` themselves. This is simple for single-entity use cases. A use case that changes several aggregates in one transaction needs a unit of work instead.

# AGENTS.md for the API layer

These rules apply to code in `src/Api`, in addition to the root `AGENTS.md`. They cover HTTP endpoints and the composition root.

## What lives here

- `Program.cs`: the composition root. It reads configuration, registers the services of the other layers, and maps the endpoints.
- `Endpoints/`: one static class per feature (for example `TodoEndpoints`) with a `Map...Endpoints` extension method, and the request types for that feature.

The sample uses minimal APIs. The rules below apply to controllers too, unless they say otherwise.

## Boundaries

- An endpoint does three things: validate the input, call the application layer, and map the result to an HTTP response. Why: business rules in an endpoint cannot be reused or unit tested without HTTP.
- Do not use EF Core, a `DbContext`, or a repository in this project. Call an application service instead. An architecture test (`ApiDoesNotUseEntityFramework`) fails the build when EF Core is used here.
- Do not use domain entities in this project. Accept request types defined here and return the DTOs that the application layer returns. Why: returning an entity exposes every field it has, now and in the future, and ties the public contract to the domain model. An architecture test (`ApiDoesNotUseDomain`) enforces this.
- `Infrastructure` is referenced for one purpose: calling `AddInfrastructure` and `ApplyMigrationsAsync` in `Program.cs`. Do not use anything else from it.
- Keep request types and endpoint classes `internal`. Nothing outside this project needs them.

## Endpoints

- Group the endpoints of a feature with `MapGroup` and register them from one `Map...Endpoints` method. `Program.cs` only calls that method.
- Write handlers as named `private static` methods, not inline lambdas. Why: named methods keep `MapPost` and `MapGet` lines readable and show up by name in stack traces.
- Return `TypedResults`, and declare every possible response in the return type, for example `Task<Results<Ok<TodoDto>, NotFound>>`. Why: the compiler then rejects a response that the signature does not declare, and the response types are visible to API description tools. Source: [Create responses in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/responses).
- Make every handler that does I/O `async`, accept a `CancellationToken`, and pass it to the application layer. Why: when the client disconnects, the request stops instead of finishing work nobody will read.
- Never call `.Result` or `.Wait()`.
- Do not catch exceptions in a handler to turn them into responses. Expected outcomes, such as "not found", are return values of the application layer. Unexpected errors go to the exception handler.

## Status codes

- `201 Created` with a `Location` header for a successful create.
- `200 OK` for a successful read.
- `400 Bad Request` with validation problem details when the input is invalid.
- `404 Not Found` when the resource does not exist.
- Do not return `200 OK` with an error message in the body.

## Validation

- Validate everything that comes from the request before calling the application layer. Request properties are nullable (`string?`) because a client can omit any of them.
- Return validation errors with `TypedResults.ValidationProblem`, keyed by the name of the field.
- Do not copy limits into this project. Read them from the application layer, as `TodoService.MaxTitleLength` does. Why: a copied number drifts when the rule changes.
- Validation here is for a clear error message. It does not replace the rules in the domain entity, which stay in place for every caller.

## Errors

- Errors use problem details ([RFC 9457](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457)). `AddProblemDetails` and `UseExceptionHandler` are registered in `Program.cs`. Do not remove them.
- Never put a stack trace, an exception message, a SQL statement, or a connection string in a response. See `SECURITY.md`.

## Authentication and authorization

- The sample endpoints are anonymous on purpose, because the sample has no users. This is a decision for the sample, not a default to copy.
- When you add an endpoint, state in the pull request who may call it. If the project has authentication, require it on the route group and opt out per endpoint, not the other way round. Why: a forgotten opt-in leaves an endpoint open, while a forgotten opt-out only fails closed.
- Never trust an identifier from the request to decide what a caller may see. Check that the caller has access to that record.

## Configuration

- Read configuration in `Program.cs` and pass values to the other layers. Fail at startup with a clear message when a required value is missing, as the connection string check does.
- `appsettings.json` holds no secrets. Use user secrets or environment variables for real values.
- Migrations are applied at startup in the Development environment only. Do not widen that condition.

## Tests

- Every endpoint has integration tests in `tests/IntegrationTests` that call it over HTTP through `PlaybookApiFactory`. Cover the success response and each error response that the handler declares.
- Tests declare their own response types instead of reusing the DTOs from the application layer. Why: a test that reuses the DTO still passes when a property is renamed, although the change breaks every client.

## Opinions

These are choices of this playbook, not facts about ASP.NET Core. Adapt them to your team.

- Minimal APIs instead of controllers. Both work. Minimal APIs keep the sample small.
- Validation by hand in the handler. It is explicit and has no dependencies. With many endpoints, a validation library or the built-in validation support is less repetitive.
- No API versioning and no OpenAPI document in the sample yet. Add them before the first external client depends on the API.

# AGENTS.md for the Domain layer

These rules apply to code in `src/Domain`, in addition to the root `AGENTS.md`. They cover entities, value objects, and business rules.

## What lives here

- One folder per feature (for example `Todos/`) with its entities and value objects.
- Nothing else. No interfaces for storage, no DTOs, no services that need I/O.

## Dependencies

- This project references no other project and no NuGet package. Do not add one. Why: business rules that depend on nothing can be read, tested, and reused without a database, a web server, or a framework upgrade getting in the way. An architecture test (`DomainUsesNoOtherLayerAndNoFramework`) fails the build when this is broken.
- No EF Core attributes, no JSON attributes, no ASP.NET Core types. Mapping to tables lives in `Infrastructure`. Mapping to HTTP lives in `Api`.
- If a rule seems to need a database lookup or another service, it does not belong in an entity. Say so, and put the orchestration in the application layer.

## Entities

- An entity can never exist in an invalid state. Check every rule when the entity is created and when it changes, and throw when a rule is broken. See `TodoItem.Create`.
- Create entities through a static factory method and keep the constructor private. Why: the factory has a name that says what happens, and there is one place where the creation rules live.
- No public setters. Change state through methods that are named after what happens in the business, such as `Complete`, not `SetCompletedAt`. Why: a setter lets any caller skip the rules. An architecture test (`DomainTypesHaveNoPublicSetters`) enforces this. Init-only properties are allowed, because they cannot change after creation.
- Do not add a public parameterless constructor or a setter because a tool asks for one. EF Core and the serializers used in this solution do not need them.
- Put limits such as `MaxTitleLength` in a public constant on the entity. Other layers read the constant instead of copying the number.
- Mark classes `sealed` unless inheritance is part of the design.

## Time, identifiers, and randomness

- Never read the system clock here. No `DateTime.Now`, `DateTime.UtcNow`, `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow`, or `TimeProvider`. Take the time as a parameter, as `Create` and `Complete` do. Why: rules that depend on the current time cannot be tested reliably otherwise.
- Use `DateTimeOffset`, not `DateTime`, for points in time. Why: a `DateTime` does not say which time zone it is in.
- An entity creates its own identifier with `Guid.NewGuid()`. The database does not generate it. Why: the entity is complete before it is saved, so the application layer can return it or refer to it without a round trip.

## Errors

- Throw `ArgumentException` (or a subclass) for an invalid argument, and `InvalidOperationException` for an operation that the current state does not allow.
- Decide on purpose whether repeating an operation is an error or does nothing, and write the decision in the method's summary. `Complete` does nothing the second time.
- Do not return error codes, booleans, or `null` to signal a broken rule.

## Async and I/O

- No `async`, no `Task`, no `CancellationToken`, no logging, and no file, network, or database access in this project. Domain code is plain, synchronous, in-memory code.

## Tests

- Every rule has a unit test in `tests/UnitTests`: one for the valid case and one for each way the rule can be broken.
- Domain tests need no fakes or mocks. If one seems necessary, the code under test probably does not belong in the domain.

## Opinions

These are choices of this playbook, not facts. Adapt them to your team.

- Exceptions for broken rules instead of a result type. Exceptions keep the sample small. A result type makes expected failures explicit and is a good choice when a use case has many of them.
- Identifiers are plain `Guid` values. Strongly typed identifiers prevent mixing up the ids of different entities, at the cost of more mapping code.
- No domain events in the sample. Add them when one change must trigger work in another part of the system.

# AGENTS.md for the Application layer

These rules apply to code in `src/Application`, in addition to the root `AGENTS.md`. They cover use cases and the interfaces for everything outside the application.

## What lives here

- One folder per feature (for example `Todos/`) with its service, its DTOs, and the interfaces it needs from the outside world.
- `ApplicationServiceRegistration.cs`: registers the services of this layer.

## Dependencies

- This project references `Domain` only. It must not use `Infrastructure`, `Api`, EF Core, or ASP.NET Core. An architecture test (`ApplicationDoesNotUseInfrastructureApiOrFrameworks`) fails the build when this is broken.
- The only package is `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Abstractions`, for service registration. Do not add a package without stating why it is needed, as the root rules require.
- When a use case needs something from outside, such as storage, email, or another system, define an interface here and implement it in `Infrastructure`. See `ITodoRepository`. Why: the use case then depends on what it needs, not on how it is done, and it can be tested with a fake.
- Shape each interface around what the use cases need, with one method per need. Do not expose `IQueryable<T>`, a `DbSet<T>`, or a generic repository with methods nobody calls.

## Use cases

- A use case is one public method on a service: load what it needs, call the domain, save, and return a DTO. See `TodoService.CreateAsync`.
- Business rules live in the domain entity, not here. If you are writing an `if` about what is allowed, it probably belongs in `Domain`. This layer decides the order of the steps.
- Do not use HTTP concepts here: no status codes, no `IResult`, no `HttpContext`, no problem details. Why: the same use case must work from an endpoint, a background job, or a test.
- Do not read the system clock directly. Inject `TimeProvider` and pass the time to the domain, as `TodoService` does. Source: [TimeProvider](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/standard/datetime/timeprovider-overview).
- Services are `sealed`, get their dependencies through the constructor, and hold no state between calls.

## What goes in and what comes out

- Never return a domain entity from a use case. Return a DTO, such as `TodoDto`. Why: the caller would otherwise be able to change the entity outside a use case, and every field of the entity would become part of the public contract. The architecture test `ApiDoesNotUseDomain` fails when an entity reaches the API.
- DTOs are `sealed record` types with no behavior besides mapping from an entity.
- Take simple values or a request record as input, not an entity and not an API request type.
- Return `null` (as `GetAsync` does) or a result value for an expected outcome such as "not found". Do not throw for outcomes the caller is expected to handle.

## Async

- Every method that reaches I/O through an interface is `async`, ends in `Async`, takes a `CancellationToken` as its last parameter, and passes it on. The token has no default value. Why: a default lets a caller forget it without the compiler noticing.
- Never call `.Result` or `.Wait()`.
- Do not start work that outlives the request with `Task.Run` or a discarded task.

## Registration

- Register every service of this layer in `AddApplication`. `Api` calls that method and registers nothing from this layer by itself.
- Use the scoped lifetime for services, because they depend on scoped storage.

## Tests

- Every use case has unit tests in `tests/UnitTests`, with hand-written fakes for the interfaces (see `FakeTodoRepository`) and a fixed clock (see `FixedTimeProvider`).
- Unit tests here do not use a database or HTTP. Tests of the real storage are in `tests/IntegrationTests`.

## Opinions

These are choices of this playbook, not facts. Adapt them to your team.

- One service class per feature with a method per use case. A handler class per use case (often with a mediator library) is a common alternative. It gives smaller classes at the cost of more files and, with a library, one more dependency.
- Hand-written fakes instead of a mocking library. They keep the tests readable and add no package. A mocking library pays off when interfaces are large.
- Mapping by hand in a static method on the DTO, with no mapping library. The compiler then catches a missing property.

# AGENTS.md for the tests

These rules apply to code in `tests/`, in addition to the root `AGENTS.md`. They cover what to test, where, and how.

## What lives here

| Project | What it tests | What it may use |
|---|---|---|
| `UnitTests` | Domain rules and application use cases | Plain objects, hand-written fakes, a fixed clock. No database, no HTTP, no file system. |
| `IntegrationTests` | The API over HTTP and the data access code | The real API in memory and a real temporary SQLite database |
| `ArchitectureTests` | The dependency and design rules from the `AGENTS.md` files | Reflection over the compiled assemblies |

- `Directory.Build.props` in this folder adds the test packages to every test project. Do not add them to a project file.
- `Shared/TestConventionTests.cs` is compiled into every test project and checks the tests of that project.

## Never weaken a test

- Never skip, delete, comment out, or loosen a test to get a green build. If a test fails, the code or the test is wrong. Find out which, and fix that. Why: a weakened test still looks like coverage, so nobody notices the gap.
- The test `NoTestIsSkipped` fails when a test or a data row has `Skip` set. It cannot see a test that was deleted or commented out. Reviewers must look for those in the diff.
- If you believe a test is wrong, say why in the pull request and change the test in a way that still checks the behavior.

## What to test

- Every change in behavior comes with a test that fails without the change.
- Test behavior through the public surface: the methods of an entity, the methods of a service, the HTTP endpoints. Do not test private methods, and do not assert on how the code reaches its result. Why: tests tied to implementation details break on every refactoring and stop people from improving the code.
- Cover the valid case and each way a rule can be broken. Cover the boundary, as `CreateAcceptsATitleOfExactlyTheMaximumLength` does.
- Put the test at the lowest level that can prove the behavior. A domain rule is a unit test. A status code or a database mapping is an integration test.
- A rule that can be checked by reflection belongs in `ArchitectureTests`, so the build enforces it instead of a reviewer.

## How to write a test

- Name a test as a sentence about the behavior, in PascalCase, without underscores: `GetReturnsNullForAnUnknownId`. The name must make sense in a failure report without opening the file.
- One behavior per test. Several assertions are fine when they describe the same outcome.
- Structure a test as arrange, act, assert, separated by blank lines. No `if`, loops, or `try`/`catch` in a test.
- Use `[Theory]` with `[InlineData]` when the same behavior is checked with different inputs.
- Test classes are `public sealed`. Helpers and fakes are `internal sealed`.
- Use literal expected values. Do not compute the expected value with the same logic as the code under test.

## Determinism

- A test gives the same result every time, on every machine, in any order.
- Never read the real clock. Use `FixedTimeProvider` and fixed `DateTimeOffset` values.
- No `Thread.Sleep`, no `Task.Delay`, and no retries to make a test pass. A test that needs to wait is waiting for something specific. Await that instead.
- No shared mutable state between tests. Each test creates what it needs. xUnit creates a new instance of the test class for every test, so instance fields are safe and static fields are not.
- Tests do not call real external services and do not need network access.

## Fakes

- Replace an interface of the application layer with a hand-written fake, such as `FakeTodoRepository`. Keep the fake as simple as an in-memory collection.
- Fake only what you own: the interfaces defined in `Application`. Do not fake `DbContext`, `HttpClient`, or framework types.
- Do not add a mocking library without the justification that the root rules require for any new package.

## Integration tests

- Use `PlaybookApiFactory` to run the API. It gives each test class its own temporary database and applies the migrations.
- Do not use the EF Core in-memory provider. Why: it does not run SQL, so it hides translation errors and constraint violations.
- Declare the response types a test reads inside the test class. Do not reuse the DTOs of the application layer. Why: a test that reuses the DTO still passes when a property is renamed, although the change breaks every client.
- Assert on the status code first, then on the body.
- A test cleans up what it creates outside the process, as `TemporaryDatabase` deletes its file.

## Architecture tests

- When you add a rule to an `AGENTS.md` that can be checked automatically, add the check in the same pull request.
- Prove that a new check can fail: break the rule on purpose, see the test fail, and undo the change. Say in the pull request that you did. Why: a check that can never fail protects nothing.
- Failure messages name the offending type or member, so the fix is obvious.

## Running the tests

- `dotnet test --no-build` from the repository root runs every test on both target frameworks. All of them must pass before a change is finished.

## Opinions

These are choices of this playbook, not facts. Adapt them to your team.

- xUnit as the test framework. NUnit, MSTest, and TUnit work as well. The rules above do not depend on the framework, except for the `Skip` check.
- The assertions that come with xUnit, with no assertion library.
- No code coverage threshold. A threshold is easy to satisfy with tests that assert nothing. The rule "every change in behavior has a test that fails without it" is checked in review instead.
- Test names without underscores. `Method_State_Result` is a common alternative.
